source_report: English edition of '벼 옥수수 병해 특징 서술 출처' (Korean)
note: One feature row = one feature from one source. Descriptions are English renderings of Korean paraphrases; quotes are 15 words or fewer. 'Unconfirmed' marks unverified items.

diseases.intro: No Korean source confirmed. No Nongsaro page for northern leaf blight (geuleummunui-byeong or ipmareum-byeong) was found and the dynamic NCPMS page did not open. Below are US extension sources and a paper on Indian isolates.

features.description: Early lesions are small, light-colored and oval. They form along leaf margins or parallel to the veins, with diffuse, water-soaked edges.
features.short_quote: "small, light-colored elliptical lesions… diffuse margin and a water-soaked appearance"
features.source_name: CPN, An Overview of Northern Corn Leaf Blight

features.description: Lesions keep enlarging up to 6 in (about 15 cm), crossing veins to become typically 'cigar-shaped'. Over time they turn gray to tan.
features.source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

features.description: Long elliptical lesions 1–6 in long. Gray-green at first, later light gray or tan.
features.short_quote: "long (1 to 6 inches) and elliptical, gray-green at first"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Northern Corn Leaf Blight of Corn

features.description: Relatively large gray or gray-green elliptical to cigar-shaped lesions, 1 in to more than 6 in long, lying parallel to the veins. On some hybrids lesions may have dark borders. Not limited by veins, and no wound is needed for infection.
features.source_name: Nebraska Extension NebGuide G2270, Northern Corn Leaf Blight (T. A. Jackson-Ziems, 2016)

features.description: On hybrids with Ht genes, lesions are small and chlorotic and may develop as linear streaks. Such lesions produce few spores.
features.short_quote: "smaller, chlorotic, and may develop into linear streaks"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

features.description: On hybrids with partial (non-race-specific) resistance, lesions are small, restricted and sporulate little. They appear as narrow yellow or chlorotic streaks rather than cigar shapes and are easily missed.
features.source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

features.description: On seed inbreds or some resistant hybrids, lesions may be smaller, more yellow, or produce no spores.
features.short_quote: "smaller, more yellow, and/or not produce spores"
features.source_name: NebGuide G2270

features.description: Lesions may also form on ear husks, but kernels are not infected.
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

features.description: Besides leaves, lesions also form on husks and leaf sheaths.
features.source_name: NebGuide G2270

features.description: Under humid conditions dark gray spores form mainly on the **leaf underside**, making lesions look 'dirty gray'.
features.short_quote: "usually on the lower leaf surface… 'dirty' gray appearance"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

features.description: In the center of mature lesions, dark gray-green spores are borne at the tips of hyphae, not enclosed in other fruiting structures. They can be seen with a hand lens or a smartphone camera at ×20. They are easiest to see after dew or rain and hard to see on dry or old lesions.
features.short_quote: "dark gray-green spores… not confined within another fungal structure"
features.source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

features.description: As lesions mature they turn tan, and spores forming in the middle of the lesion make it look darker and dusty.
features.source_name: NebGuide G2270

features.description: In fields with heavy residue it appears first on lower leaves because of spores spread by rain splash and wind. Under suitable conditions it progresses to middle and upper leaves. It may also appear first on upper leaves from windblown spores from neighboring fields. On susceptible hybrids lesions merge and whole leaves dry.
features.short_quote: "may also be observed first in the upper canopy"
features.source_name: CPN Overview NCLB
features.location_in_source: 'When symptoms appear' paragraph; end of 'Symptoms' first paragraph

features.description: Starts with a few scattered lesions on lower leaves and spreads to upper leaves as favorable conditions continue. One or more lesions form per leaf and enlarge, drying the leaf.
features.short_quote: "a few lesions scattered in the lower canopy"
features.source_name: NebGuide G2270

features.description: Can appear at any time in the season, but is usually observed from the late vegetative stage (V10–V14) to physiological maturity (R6). Under suitable conditions lesions appear within 1 week of infection.
features.source_name: CPN Overview NCLB

features.description: Favored by leaf wetness over 6 hours and 18–27 °C (64–81 °F).
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia NCLB

features.description: Spores need 6–18 hours of water on the leaf surface to germinate. High humidity and mild temperatures are favorable.
features.short_quote: "6–18 hours of water on the leaf surface"
features.source_name: NebGuide G2270

features.description: Conidia are elongated and fusiform with a **protruding hilum**. They have 2–12 septa (most isolates 3–6, 3–7, 3–8 or 3–9). Conidia are 52.94–144.12 µm long and 10.0–25.88 µm wide. Shapes were described as elongated elliptical, obclavate to fusiform, slightly curved (45 isolates from Bihar, India).
features.source_name: Anwer et al. 2022, Bioengineering 9(8):403 (PMC9405478)
features.location_in_source: Abstract; 3.1 Cultural and Morphological Characterization; Table 1; Fig. 3

features.description: Colonies after 10 days on PDA fall into four groups: olive-brown, blackish-brown, whitish-black and gray. Colony forms include flat and cottony-raised, with regular or irregular margins.
features.short_quote: "olivaceous brown, blackish brown, whitish black, and grayish"
features.source_name: Anwer et al. 2022

features.description: β-tubulin gene sequences confirmed isolate identity and phylogenetic relationships.
features.source_name: Anwer et al. 2022

source_conflicts: Sporulation surface: the CPN encyclopedia says 'mainly the leaf underside', while the same organization's CPN Overview and NebGuide G2270 say only 'lesion center'.
Lesion borders: the CPN Overview describes early edges as 'diffuse, water-soaked' and G2270 as 'dark borders on some hybrids', so borders are hard to use as a diagnostic criterion.
Lesion length agrees across all three English sources at 1–6 in (up to more than 6 in); no width figure is given anywhere.

The only conidial figures come from 45 isolates in Bihar, India (Anwer 2022), and septum variation (2–12) is large, so they are hard to use as standard values. Standard descriptions such as the APS Compendium were not obtained.
The small chlorotic streaks of resistant reaction types (Ht genes, partial resistance) resemble southern corn leaf blight, so CPN recommends laboratory diagnosis.
diseases.photo_visible: Cigar-shaped lesions 2.5–15 cm long not limited by veins, gray-green turning tan, progression from lower to upper leaves, dark gray spores in the lesion center under humid conditions (×20 close-up photo).
diseases.lab_required: Fusiform conidia with protruding hilum and septum number (microscopy), separation from resistant reaction types and southern corn leaf blight, β-tubulin sequencing (molecular).

diseases.intro: There are Korean official descriptions (Nongsaro, RDA press release 2025), but they come from the same agency group, give the same size figures and cite no original literature. In Korea it is called 'kkaessimunui-byeong' (the same name as rice brown spot). Pathogen morphology figures appear only in an overseas taxonomic monograph.

features.description: Small pale-brown spots form, with slightly darker brown margins. Lesions spread between veins, and many are about 0.5 cm wide and 1–2 cm long.
features.source_name: Nongsaro pest information 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)' (RDA)

features.description: Race T lesions are yellow-brown, 0.6–1.2 cm wide and 0.6–2.7 cm long. They may become fusiform or elliptical with yellow-green or white rings. Race O usually attacks only leaves.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

features.description: Elliptical pale-brown 'sesame-seed spots' 0.5 cm wide and 1–2 cm long form on leaves. As disease intensifies, symptoms enlarge and leaves dry.
features.source_name: RDA press release "Maize diseases need different control methods by type" (2025-06-16, National Institute of Crop Science)

features.description: Race O lesions are tan, somewhat rectangular, with reddish-brown borders.
features.short_quote: "tan, somewhat rectangular in shape… reddish-brown margins"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Southern Corn Leaf Blight of Corn

features.description: Race T lesions are rectangular to elliptical, ¼–½ in (about 0.6–1.3 cm) wide and ¼–¾ in (about 0.6–1.9 cm) long. There may be a chlorotic zone around the reddish-brown border.
features.short_quote: "¼ to ½ inch wide by ¼ to ¾ inch long"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

features.description: Lesions vary by race but are generally tan to brown rectangles with brown borders, often with yellow halos. They are smaller than NCLB lesions and stay on lower leaves. They resemble NCLB resistant reaction types, so laboratory diagnosis may be needed.
features.short_quote: "rectangular lesions with a brown margin… often surrounded by a yellow halo"
features.source_name: CPN Overview NCLB (section on confusable diseases)
features.location_in_source: 'Southern corn leaf blight' look-alike subsection, Fig. 10

features.description: Leaf lesions are brown, sometimes purplish or with reddish-brown borders, occasionally with concentric rings. When they merge they turn gray. Length is 2.5 cm. They are elliptical at first, then elongate lengthwise and become rectangular when limited by veins.
features.short_quote: "becoming rectangular when spots are restricted by veins"
features.source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014, "The genus Bipolaris", Studies in Mycology 79:221-288 (PMC4255534)
features.location_in_source: *Bipolaris maydis* species description, 'Symptoms on Zea mays'

features.description: Later, race T lesions form on leaves, stalks and sheaths, with dark black to reddish-brown margins. With any race, early leaf infection readily leads to stalk rot.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

features.description: Race T attacks leaves, husks, stalks, sheaths, ear shanks, ears and cobs. Stalk and leaf infections start as purple spots whose centers become tan to gray.
features.short_quote: "initially appear as purple spots that develop tan-gray centers"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

features.description: Infected kernels can be covered with black mold. Race T causes kernel and ear rot, with large losses in grain and silage yield.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

features.description: When disease is severe, grain and shanks rot.
features.source_name: RDA press release 2025-06-16

features.description: When ears are infected, gray-black lesions form on husks and spread to kernels, appearing as black felt-like mold.
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

features.description: Seedlings from infected seed may wilt and die within 3–4 weeks after sowing.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

features.description: Seedlings from infected kernels often wilt.
features.short_quote: "Seedlings from infected kernels are often blighted"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia SCLB

features.description: Under suitable conditions, disease development is complete in about 60–72 hours. It overwinters as spores or mycelium in diseased residue, and infected grain is also an important overwintering structure. Primary and secondary spread is by wind and rain splash.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

features.description: Inland it mainly occurs in hot, humid summers (June–August). On Jeju, where planting is early, it may occur in tunnel cultivation due to high temperatures inside the tunnels.
features.source_name: RDA press release 2025-06-16

features.description: Damage is great in warm, humid weather at 20–30 °C. Race T occurs more readily than race O in northern areas and is scarce in the dry season with little rain.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

features.description: On normal-cytoplasm maize, race T and race O are hard to distinguish reliably by symptoms. Race T is pathogenic to maize with the Tm-sc gene (T-type male-sterile cytoplasm) and causes smaller lesions on ordinary maize. Race O shows no differential reaction between cytoplasm types.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

features.description: (PDA culture) Conidiophores are (90–)105–470(–712) × 5–7 µm, solitary or in small groups, usually unbranched, septate, olive-brown and geniculate near the top. Conidiogenous nodes are distinctly dark brown.
features.source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014 (PMC4255534)
features.location_in_source: *B. maydis* species description 'Asexual morph on PDA', Fig. 22F–I

features.description: Conidia are (59–)66–102(–160) × (12–)14–18(–20) µm (mean 94 × 16 µm, n=100), pale to medium dark brown, smooth, slightly curved fusiform, with (5–)8(–11) **distosepta**. The hilum is distinct, 3–5 µm wide, and germ tubes arise from both ends of the spore (bipolar). Secondary conidiation is occasionally observed.
features.source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014

features.description: Perithecia are (198–)225–459(–600) µm in diameter and black. Ascospores are filiform, 130–340 × 6–9 µm, 5–9-septate and tightly coiled in the ascus (Sach's agar).
features.source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014

features.description: Colonies on PDA are grayish-white when young and black when mature.
features.source_name: Manamgoda et al. 2014

features.description: The Nongsaro page gives only the scientific name (*C. heterostrophus*) and no description of conidia or conidiophores. Morphometrics of Korean isolates: **Unconfirmed**.
features.source_name: Nongsaro 'Southern corn leaf blight (kkaessimunui-byeong)'

source_conflicts: Lesion shape terms: Korean sources emphasize 'spots spreading between veins', race T 'fusiform/elliptical' and 'elliptical sesame-seed spots', while English sources emphasize race O 'somewhat rectangular', race T 'rectangular to elliptical' and Manamgoda 'rectangular when limited by veins'.

Size: Nongsaro and RDA give 0.5 cm wide and 1–2 cm long, and Nongsaro race T 0.6–1.2 × 0.6–2.7 cm. CPN race T is about 0.6–1.3 × 0.6–1.9 cm, and Manamgoda gives 2.5 cm long. The Korean race T maximum length exceeds CPN's, and whether it is a Korean measurement cannot be confirmed.
Halo and rings: Nongsaro race T 'yellow-green or white rings', CPN encyclopedia 'chlorotic zone', CPN NCLB document 'yellow halos common', Manamgoda 'occasional concentric rings'.
No corresponding statement was found in English sources for Nongsaro's 'race T occurs readily in northern areas'.
The Nongsaro and RDA figures (0.5 cm wide, 1–2 cm long) repeat each other within the same agency group, so they are hard to treat as independent evidence.
diseases.photo_visible: Small tan elongated-oval to rectangular lesions confined between veins (about 0.5 cm wide) with reddish-brown borders, gray-black lesions on ear husks and black felt-like mold.
diseases.lab_required: Race T/O separation (reaction on T-cytoplasm differential hosts; not visually possible), distoseptate fusiform conidia germinating from both ends (microscopy), separation from NCLB resistant reaction types (laboratory).

diseases.intro: A Korean official GLS description is Unconfirmed. The 'jeommunui-byeong' (leaf spot) description in the RDA 2025 press release gives no scientific name, so it is not confirmed to be the same disease (marked 'match to disease name unconfirmed' in the table).

features.description: Early symptoms are brown or tan spots 0.2 in (about 5 mm) wide and 0.4–0.8 in (about 1–2 cm) long filling the space between veins. These lesions become irregular to rectangular, and yellow borders are **easier to see against the light**.
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902, Gray Leaf Spot of Corn

features.description: Mature lesions are tan or gray, vein-limited rectangles with blunt ends, 0.2 in (about 5 mm) wide and up to 2.8 in (about 7 cm) long. They run parallel to the veins and in severe cases merge, drying the whole leaf.
features.short_quote: "vein-limited, rectangular-shaped (0.2 inches wide and up to 2.8 inches long), with blunt-ends"
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Lesions are long (up to 2 in), narrow rectangles, light tan, later turning gray. They are usually vein-limited but can merge and kill whole leaves.
features.short_quote: "long (up to 2 inches), narrow, rectangular, and light tan colored"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Gray Leaf Spot of Corn

features.description: The typical symptom is tan to brown rectangular lesions on mature leaves, ½–2 in (about 1.3–5 cm) long and 1/8–1/4 in (about 3–6 mm) wide, long and narrow. Secondary and tertiary veins limit their width, so the sides are parallel.
features.short_quote: "long (1/2 to 2 inches), narrow (1/8 to 1/4 inch), rectangular"
features.source_name: Purdue Extension BP-56, Gray Leaf Spot of Corn (G. E. Shaner, P. R. Sellers, D. H. Scott)

features.description: The first symptoms are small, dark, water-soaked spots, often surrounded by a narrow yellow halo. The spots enlarge quickly, the central tissue dies, and they elongate into the characteristic long, narrow lesions.
features.short_quote: "tiny, dark, water-soaked spot… narrow, yellow halo"
features.source_name: Purdue BP-56

features.description: *C. zeina* lesions form on both surfaces, are vein-limited, 2–3 mm wide and 5–40 mm long. They merge readily and are pale gray to pale brown, with indistinct borders; young lesions are chlorotic.
features.short_quote: "Leaf spots amphigenous, vein-limited, 2–3 mm wide, 5–40 mm long"
features.source_name: Crous et al. 2006, Studies in Mycology 55:189-197 (PMC2104713)

features.description: *C. zeae-maydis* lesions are oblong and often become elongated streaks or irregular gray to brown spots. Size and shape vary, and narrow brown borders are common.
features.source_name: Crous et al. 2006

features.description: Sheath symptoms are relatively large round to oblong tan to dark-brown lesions surrounded by dark-brown to dark-purple borders. They are hard to distinguish from lesions of the NCLB, SCLB and northern corn leaf spot pathogens.
features.source_name: Purdue BP-56

features.description: Stalk infection has been reported, and severe cases cause lodging. Sheath and husk lesions may be elliptical and are usually not diagnostic.
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Husk lesions resemble leaf lesions in shape.
features.short_quote: "Husk lesions are similar in appearance to leaf lesions"
features.source_name: Purdue BP-56

features.description: Gray spores emerge from mature lesions, which is the origin of the disease name.
features.short_quote: "release of gray fungal spores… gives the disease its name"
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Lesions are tan at first and take on a gray color when many spores form on the lesion surface.
features.short_quote: "may become grayish when the fungus produces numerous spores"
features.source_name: Purdue BP-56

features.description: Up to 5,000 conidia form per mm² of a typical lesion, of which 50–80% can germinate.
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Conidiophore fascicles (caespituli) form on both surfaces but mainly on the leaf underside. They are punctiform to slightly spreading and brown.
features.source_name: Crous et al. 2006

features.description: Stromata in overwintered residue produce conidia, which reach the lower leaves of the new crop by wind and rain splash. They enter through stomata within 4–7 days, and chlorosis appears about 9 days after infection. Secondary conidia form 14–21 days after inoculation. The infection cycle is 14–21 days on susceptible hybrids and 21–28 days on tolerant hybrids.
features.short_quote: "Chlorotic symptoms can develop in about nine days"
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Tolerant hybrids produce chlorotic or fleck-type lesions, while susceptible hybrids produce elongated necrotic lesions.
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Symptoms first appear on lower leaves about 2–3 weeks before tasseling.
features.short_quote: "first appear on lower leaves about two to three weeks before tasseling"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia GLS

features.description: Under favorable conditions symptoms usually appear 2–4 weeks before pollination.
features.short_quote: "two to four weeks prior to pollination"
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Requires at least 12 hours of free moisture and RH of 90% or above. The original gives temperature as '70–90 °F/25–32 °C' (70 °F is about 21 °C, so the conversion is wrong).
features.short_quote: "at least 12 hours of free moisture… ≥90 percent"
features.source_name: UNL NebGuide G1902

features.description: Infection and development are favored by warm weather (80s °F) and humid weather with RH of 90% or above lasting more than 12 hours.
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia GLS

features.description: Conidiophores emerge through stomata in fascicles of 3–14, 40–180 × 4–8 µm, with (0–)1–8 septa, pale olive to medium brown and geniculate. Conidiogenous loci are thickened and darkened, 2–3 µm wide. Conidia are solitary, broadly obclavate to subcylindrical, 30–100 × 4–9 µm, 1–10-septate and hyaline. The apex is obtuse and the base obconically truncate, with a slightly thickened, darkened hilum 2–3 µm wide.
features.source_name: Crous et al. 2006

features.description: Conidiophores form loose fascicles of 3–20, 40–100 × 5–7 µm, 1–5-septate. Conidiogenous cells are 40–60 × 5–6 µm, and loci are thickened, darkened, refractive and 2–3 µm wide. Conidia are broadly fusiform, (40–)60–75(–100) × (6–)7–8(–9) µm, (1–)3–5(–10)-septate and hyaline, with a thickened, darkened hilum 2–3 µm wide.
features.source_name: Crous et al. 2006

features.description: *C. zeae-maydis*: colonies 15–25 mm in diameter after 3 weeks on PDA; on OA the surface turns red (red cercosporin pigment). *C. zeina*: grows more slowly, 10–15 mm after 3 weeks on PDA, with no red pigment. On MEA both species are olive-gray with iron-gray reverse.
features.source_name: Crous et al. 2006
features.location_in_source: 'Cultural characteristics' and Notes for both species

features.description: Conidial sizes of the two species are similar. *C. zeae-maydis* has longer conidiophores (up to 180 µm vs 100 µm) and obclavate conidia, while *C. zeina* has fusiform conidia. Species are separated by culture growth rate, red pigment and multigene sequencing.
features.source_name: Crous et al. 2006

features.description: The RDA 2025 press release describes 'jeommunui-byeong' (leaf spot) as gray to yellow-brown rectangular symptoms on leaves, sometimes with yellow round dot-like symptoms. It says the disease was rare in Korea in the past but is now spreading. **With no scientific name given, whether it is the same disease as GLS is Unconfirmed**.
features.source_name: RDA press release 2025-06-16
features.source_type: Korean official (match to disease name unconfirmed)

source_conflicts: Lesion width: UNL 0.2 in (about 5 mm), Purdue 1/8–1/4 in (about 3–6 mm), and Crous's *C. zeina* description 2–3 mm; the original paper is narrower than the extension sources.
Lesion length: UNL up to 2.8 in (about 7 cm), CPN up to 2 in, Purdue ½–2 in, Crous *C. zeina* 5–40 mm.
Early symptoms: UNL 'brown or tan spots with yellow borders (against light)', Purdue 'small dark water-soaked spots with narrow yellow halos'.
Purdue describes sheath lesions specifically as 'large, round to oblong, with dark-purple borders', while UNL says only 'elliptical, not diagnostic'.
The three US extension sources use only *C. zeae-maydis* and do not distinguish *C. zeina*.
Temperature notation error: UNL G1902 writes '70–90 °F/25–32 °C', but 70 °F is about 21 °C.
The RDA 'jeommunui-byeong' phrase 'sometimes yellow round dot-like' does not appear in English GLS descriptions.
diseases.photo_visible: Narrow, long, vein-limited rectangular lesions (parallel sides, blunt ends), tan turning gray, yellow borders visible against the light.
diseases.lab_required: Hyaline conidia with thickened, darkened hilum (microscopy), separation of *C. zeae-maydis* and *C. zeina* (culture growth rate, red pigment, multigene sequencing), definitive diagnosis of sheath lesions.

diseases.intro: There is a Korean official source (Nongsaro 'rust') and an original paper on Korean specimens (Lee 2025), but the Nongsaro description conflicts with both the English sources and the Korean original paper.

features.description: Appears mainly on leaves. Diseased leaves become mottled and senesce. Yellow to orange 'aecia' (as worded in the source) form on the leaf **underside**, and small yellow to yellowish-white lesions form on the surface of lower leaves.
features.short_quote: "yellow to orange aecia (as worded) form on the leaf underside" (translated from Korean)
features.source_name: Nongsaro pest information 'Rust (銹病, Rust)' (pathogen *Puccinia sorghi*; crop not named)

features.description: The first symptom is chlorotic flecks on the leaf surface. Soon spores break through the epidermis to form powdery brick-red pustules.
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Common Rust of Corn

features.description: Pustules are oval or elongated, about 1/8 in (about 3 mm) long. They occur sparsely scattered or in clusters. Tissue around pustules yellows or dies, forming necrotic lesions, sometimes as bands across the leaf. With age the red spores turn black so pustules look black.
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust

features.description: Yellow spots quickly develop into oval to elongated reddish-brown powdery pustules. Pustules rupture the epidermis so leaves look bumpy. Pustules are usually 1/8 in long, single or in groups, with torn epidermis around them. Dark reddish-brown pustules are scattered on **both upper and lower leaf surfaces** and turn dark brown to black with age.
features.short_quote: "scattered over both the upper and lower surfaces" (Fig. 1 caption)
features.source_name: Cornell Vegetables, Common Rust of Sweet Corn (Cornell University)

features.description: Common rust pustules are raised, brick-red to brown, turn black with age, and spores rub off. They are less dense than southern rust. They form on **both leaf surfaces** and are abundant in the lower to middle canopy. No chlorotic halo is described.
features.source_name: CPN, An Overview of Southern Rust (CPN-2009, 2019)
features.location_in_source: Table 1; 'Southern rust vs. common rust' section; Fig. 7

features.description: On Korean *P. sorghi* specimens, uredinia and telia appeared on **both upper and lower leaf surfaces**. Uredinia are reddish-brown and oblong (Results 3.1), summarized in the Discussion as 'circular uredinia'. Telia are blackish-brown, fusiform to linear.
features.short_quote: "Uredinia and telia appeared on both adaxial and abaxial leaf surfaces"
features.source_name: Lee YK et al. 2025, Mycobiology 53(5):637-647 (PMC12337728)

features.description: Husks, sheaths and stalks can also be infected. Pustules also form on the leaf midrib (photo caption).
features.short_quote: "Husks, leaf sheaths, and stalks also may be infected"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust
features.location_in_source: Body first paragraph; photo caption 'on leaf midrib'

features.description: (US Midwest) Pustules usually first appear in late June.
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust

features.description: Often starts at the late vegetative stage (southern rust after VT).
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

features.description: The 4 Korean *P. sorghi* specimens are 3 from Gangwon (1992) and 1 from Jeonbuk (2021), all collected in late autumn (October–November).
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Favored by high humidity, daytime temperatures of 60–77 °F and night temperatures of 65–70 °F. Leaves must be wet for at least 3 hours for infection. In New York it does not overwinter and blows in from the south each year. In the tropics and subtropics it completes its life cycle on the alternate host *Oxalis*.
features.short_quote: "requires leaves to be wet for at least 3 hours"
features.source_name: Cornell Common Rust

features.description: Urediniospores from Korean specimens are globose to subglobose or ovoid and **brown**, 22–35 × 23–34 µm (mean 29 × 26 µm, n=30), with echinulate walls.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Teliospores from Korean specimens are oblong or obovoid, 31–40 × 18–26 µm (mean 36 × 21 µm, n=100).
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Common rust spores are brick-red, while southern rust spores are more orange (photo caption).
features.short_quote: "Common rust spores… brick red… southern rust spores… more orange"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust

features.description: Common rust spores are darker and rounder; southern rust spores are lighter and slightly elongated.
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

features.description: A heteroecious rust fungus requiring *Oxalis* species as the alternate host. Under favorable conditions it is associated with 18–49% yield loss.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Phylogenetic analysis of ITS, LSU rDNA and COX3 mtDNA separates it into a clade distinct from *P. polysora*. For old specimens only ITS1 was amplified with PsorF/PsorR.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

source_conflicts: Surface of occurrence (suspected major error): Nongsaro says 'yellow to orange aecia on the leaf underside', but CPN Table 1, Cornell Fig. 1 and Lee 2025 (Korean specimens) all say 'both upper and lower leaf surfaces'.
Pustule color: Nongsaro 'yellow to orange', CPN 'brick-red to brown', Cornell and Lee 2025 'reddish-brown'. The Nongsaro color is closer to the color CPN uses for southern rust (orange to tan).

Terminology: the term Nongsaro uses ('nokpojatoe') usually refers to an aecium, whereas pustules on maize are uredinia (Lee 2025, Cornell). The Nongsaro page cites no original source and does not name the crop.
Pustule shape: CPN and Cornell say 'oval to elongated', while Lee 2025 writes 'oblong' in the Results and 'circular uredinia' in the Discussion, so the paper's own wording is inconsistent.
Spore color broadly agrees: CPN 'brick-red, darker', Lee 2025 'brown'.
diseases.photo_visible: Sparsely scattered reddish-brown to brick-red elongated pustules (about 3 mm) on both leaf surfaces, black telia with age.
diseases.lab_required: Globose to ovoid brown urediniospores (22–35 × 23–34 µm) and teliospores (microscopy), definitive separation from southern rust (ITS, LSU, COX3 molecular); it is safer not to use the Nongsaro description as a diagnostic criterion until its original basis is confirmed.

diseases.intro: A Korean official agency page and an official Korean name are Unconfirmed; the Korean evidence is an original paper on 33 Korean specimens (Lee 2025). This Korean paper conflicts with the US rule 'upper surface = southern rust'.

features.description: Pustules are orange to tan, round or oval, about 1/16 in (1.5 mm) in diameter. Most form on the **upper** leaf surface, and usually only chlorosis is seen on the underside. Rubbed spores leave orange to tan streaks on fingers or clothing.
features.short_quote: "Most pustules form on the upper surface" (gist)
features.source_name: CPN, An Overview of Southern Rust (Bradley et al., CPN-2009, 2019-08-01)

features.description: Secondary-infection pustules are very numerous and dense. Light green to yellow chlorotic halos are common and visible on the leaf underside.
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

features.description: Symptoms resemble common rust, but pustules are smaller and form **almost only on the upper leaf surface**. They are usually round or oval, very numerous and densely scattered over the leaf surface. Spores are orange when they erupt. With age pustules turn chocolate-brown to black and may form dark rings around the original pustules.
features.short_quote: "occur almost exclusively on the upper leaf surface"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia, Southern Rust of Corn

features.description: On Korean specimens, uredinial symptoms appeared on **both upper and lower leaf surfaces** and rarely on stalks. Uredinia are oval or round, varying from yellow to brown. Systemic infection and chlorotic lesions were also observed as field symptoms.
features.short_quote: "Uredinial symptoms appeared on both adaxial and abaxial leaf surfaces"
features.source_name: Lee YK et al. 2025, Mycobiology 53(5):637-647 (PMC12337728)

features.description: In Korean field surveys, *P. polysora* often formed uredinia on both leaf surfaces like *P. sorghi*. Therefore an earlier poster report (Gunwi) that identified southern rust only from upper-surface predominance has limited reliability.
features.short_quote: "often formed uredinia on both leaf surfaces, similar to P. sorghi"
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Uredinia on Michigan (USA) specimens are mainly clustered on the upper leaf surface. They are pale cinnamon-brown to bright orange, ovoid and surrounded by yellow halos.
features.short_quote: "aggregated primarily on the upper leaf surface"
features.source_name: "First Report of Southern Rust (Puccinia polysora) on Corn (Zea mays) in Michigan", Plant Disease (2022) — AGRIS abstract

features.description: Pustules on specimens from Tianjin, China are randomly scattered on leaves, cinnamon to tan. They were found mainly on upper leaves and rarely on ear husks. No teliospores were found.
features.source_name: Liu X et al. 2018, Plant Disease 102(4):826 "Occurrence of Puccinia polysora… Northeast Huanghuaihai Region of China" — AGRIS abstract

features.description: Old pustules may become brown to black telia. They resemble tar spot perithecia, so laboratory confirmation may be needed.
features.short_quote: "Later in the season, the fungus forms darker pustules called telia" (encyclopedia caption)
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust; CPN Encyclopedia Southern Rust
features.location_in_source: 'Symptoms and Signs', Fig. 2; encyclopedia photo caption

features.description: In severe cases pustules also form on husks, leaf sheaths and ear shanks.
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

features.description: Pustules usually first appear in the middle to upper canopy, often starting in isolated hot spots near field ends or edges. Under favorable conditions the time from infection to sporulation can be as short as 9 days, and one pustule sporulates for up to 8 days. Young leaves are more susceptible than mature leaves.
features.short_quote: "first observed in the middle or upper plant canopy"
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

features.description: Usually appears after tasseling (VT). Late-planted or double-cropped maize is at greater risk.
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

features.description: The 33 Korean *P. polysora* specimens (Gangwon 2, Chungbuk 2, Chungnam 3, Jeonbuk 23, Jeonnam 3) were mainly collected in September and October (2021–2024).
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Infection can occur after about 6 hours of leaf wetness, and dew is often enough. High relative humidity and about 80 °F (27 °C) are favorable. It needs living green tissue and cannot overwinter in the north.
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

features.description: Urediniospore germination was highest at 25 °C (49%) and similar at 20–30 °C. It fell sharply above 32 °C and was under 2% at 38 and 40 °C. At 25–28 °C more than 40% germinated within 9 hours.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Urediniospores are light brown, ellipsoid or subglobose, 25–40 × 17–29 µm (mean 33 × 24 µm, n=30), with **hyaline echinulate walls**.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Urediniospores are yellow to golden in the center and hyaline along the outer membrane, ellipsoid to obovoid with short echinulations (light microscope ×40), 17–28 × 26–38 µm (n=180). Telia were not observed. Identity was confirmed by 28S rDNA.
features.short_quote: "hyaline along the outer membrane, ellipsoid to obovoid"
features.source_name: Plant Disease 2022 Michigan new record (AGRIS abstract)

features.description: Urediniospores are yellowish, subglobose or globose, yellow to golden, 25.0–30.0 × 28.0–37.0 µm, with echinulate surfaces. No teliospores were found.
features.short_quote: "subglobose or globose showing yellow or golden color"
features.source_name: Liu et al. 2018, Plant Disease (AGRIS abstract)

features.description: The text says telia were not observed on Korean specimens. However, the Fig. 2(P) caption reads "SEM image of telia", so there is an **internal inconsistency in the paper**.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Since the uredinial and telial stages have been observed only on maize and no alternate host is known, it may be autoecious, but this is not confirmed.
features.short_quote: "plausible that the species exhibits an autoecious life cycle"
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Phylogenetic analysis of ITS, LSU rDNA and COX3 mtDNA separates it into a clade distinct from *P. sorghi*. This study is the first to use COX3 for phylogenetic analysis of maize rusts.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2025

features.description: Southern rust can be confirmed in the diagnostic lab by identifying *P. polysora* spores under the microscope.
features.source_name: CPN Overview Southern Rust

source_conflicts: Surface of occurrence (key conflict): CPN Overview says 'mostly upper surface, chlorosis on underside', the CPN encyclopedia 'almost only upper surface', and Michigan 2022 'mainly upper surface', but Lee 2025 reported that Korean specimens often formed uredinia on 'both leaf surfaces', like *P. sorghi*. The US rule cannot be applied directly to Korean specimens.
'Upper leaves' in Liu 2018 (China) refers to canopy position (upper leaves), not the upper leaf surface.
Pustule color: CPN orange to tan, Michigan pale cinnamon-brown to bright orange, China cinnamon to tan, Lee yellow to brown.
The contrast in pustule shape runs in opposite directions. Lee contrasts '*P. polysora* oval, *P. sorghi* round' in the Discussion, while CPN calls common rust pustules 'elongated'.

Urediniospore size: Lee 25–40 × 17–29 µm, Michigan 17–28 × 26–38 µm (width × length), China 25.0–30.0 × 28.0–37.0 µm; lengths broadly overlap, and only China describes them as 'subglobose to globose'.
Telia: CPN says they form late, but Lee (text), Michigan and China did not observe them. In Lee 2025 the text's 'telia not observed' differs from the Fig. 2(P) caption 'SEM image of telia'.
diseases.photo_visible: Dense small round to oval orange to tan pustules (about 1.5 mm) with chlorotic halos, starting in the middle to upper canopy. In Korea the leaf-surface criterion does not hold.
diseases.lab_required: Light-brown ellipsoid urediniospores with hyaline echinulate walls (microscopy), ITS, LSU and COX3 molecular identification; for Korean samples in September–October, urediniospore microscopy is effectively required.

diseases.intro: There is a Korean official source (Nongsaro D00001177) and a Korean paper citing the List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004). Chlamydospore size was confirmed in only one overseas source (Illinois).

features.description: Occurs mainly on ears, stalks and leaves, and rarely on roots. Diseased parts enlarge into galls.
features.source_name: Nongsaro pests by crop: maize Common smut (D00001177)

features.description: Large galls are 10 cm or more in diameter. They are covered at first by a glossy white membrane, and when the membrane bursts, black powdery chlamydospores are released.
features.source_name: Nongsaro D00001177

features.description: Overwintered chlamydospores germinate to produce sporidia, which are carried by wind and enter tender tissue. Galls are produced only by hyphae formed by fusion of sporidia of different mating types. The latent period is 7–21 days.
features.source_name: Nongsaro D00001177

features.category: Symptoms - whole plant / timing of occurrence
features.description: Any aerial part is attacked from seedling to maturity, which distinguishes it from other grass smuts. It is most common on young, actively growing plants wounded by detasseling, hail, blowing soil, insects or machinery.
features.short_quote: "any part of the plant above ground may be attacked"
features.source_name: Univ. Illinois RPD No. 203 *Corn Smuts* (1990)

features.category: Symptoms - ear/grain / Symptoms - tassel / Symptoms - stalk
features.description: All actively growing or embryonic tissue is susceptible. Galls are common on tassels, husks, ears and kernels, stalks, leaves and axillary buds, and rare on aerial roots.
features.short_quote: "All actively growing or embryonic corn tissue is susceptible."
features.plant_part: Tassel, husks, ear, kernels, stalk, leaves, axillary buds
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: As galls enlarge they are covered by a shiny greenish-white to silvery-white membrane, and the interior darkens as spores form. Mature galls reach 15 cm (6 in) in diameter. They are filled with dark olive-brown to black, oily to powdery spores. At maturity the white outer membrane bursts and spores are released.
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Small, hard, pea-sized galls form on leaves. Unlike large galls, these are not spore masses. Leaf galls and galls at detasseling wounds are usually small and cause little damage.
features.short_quote: "small, hard, pea-sized galls that form on the leaves"
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Plants with galls on the lower stalk become sterile or bear several small ears. In autumn they look red, resembling aphid-damaged plants. Yield loss is greatest when large galls are on or above the ear.
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Chlamydospores are diploid, black, globose to subglobose and echinulate, 8–12 µm in diameter. At 10–35 °C with moisture they produce a four-celled basidium (promycelium), on which four or more ovoid sporidia of two mating types (+)/(−) form.
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Hyphae inside galls grow between cells until just before sporulation. They then invade and break down the enlarged host cells. A completed gall consists mainly of dikaryotic hyphae and host cell remnants, and only the membrane enclosing the gall is unaffected by the fungus.
features.short_quote: "Only the membrane covering the smut gall is unaffected"
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: From infection to a mature gall takes one to several weeks under suitable conditions. Spores from the first galls can reinfect the same or other plants. Gall formation and spore dispersal are almost continuous throughout the summer growing season. Ears are infected by hyphae growing along the silks.
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Infection is most severe when early-season rainfall is low and temperatures are 26–34 °C (79–93 °F). Dry periods that slow growth, and unusually cool, humid weather that slows young plants, also favor infection.
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Galls form on stalks, leaves, ears and tassels, and actively growing tissue is especially susceptible. Galls are swollen, distorted growths, covered at first by a shiny white membrane. When the membrane bursts, a blackish-brown to black powdery spore mass is exposed.
features.source_name: Crop Protection Network (CPN) Encyclopedia: Common Smut of Corn

features.description: Excess nitrogen and manure, herbicide injury, mechanical wounds, and relatively dry, warm weather favor disease. No figures are given.
features.source_name: CPN Common Smut

features.category: Symptoms - ear/grain (differentiation from other ear rots)
features.description: Kernels grow into gray tumor-like fungal masses (galls) with black spores inside, which burst when dry to release spores. Ear-rot fungi can mummify kernels or cover them with sooty spores but do not form galls. The common smut fungus forms galls on any part, including brace roots, leaves, stalks and tassels.
features.source_name: CPN-2001 *An Overview of Ear Rots* (2024 revision)

features.description: The List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004) records "smut caused by *Ustilago zeae*" as a fungal disease occurring in Korea (secondary citation in the paper's introduction).
features.source_name: Han et al. 2015, *Res. Plant Dis.* 21(4):280-289 (paper on biocontrol of stalk rot)

source_conflicts: Gall size: Nongsaro '10 cm or more', Illinois 'up to 15 cm'; only Illinois distinguishes the small, hard pea-sized galls on leaves.

Membrane color: Nongsaro 'glossy white membrane', CPN 'glistening white', Illinois 'greenish-white to silvery-white', and CPN-2001 describes ear galls as 'gray' (attributing this to maturity stage is an inference in the notes).
Spore color: Nongsaro 'black powder', Illinois 'dark olive-brown to black, oily to powdery', CPN 'blackish-brown to black'.
Latent period: Nongsaro 7–21 days, Illinois 'one to several weeks from infection to mature gall', which do not conflict.
Conditions: Illinois 'low early-season rainfall, 26–34 °C', CPN 'relatively dry and warm'; the Nongsaro detail page gives no figures.
Scientific names: Nongsaro and the List of Plant Diseases use *U. zeae*, CPN *U. maydis*, Illinois *U. zeae* (syn. *U. maydis*).
diseases.photo_visible: Fleshy swollen galls covered by a white to silvery-white membrane (ears, stalks, leaves, tassels), black powdery spores after the membrane bursts, small hard galls on leaves.
diseases.lab_required: Black globose echinulate chlamydospores 8–12 µm (microscopy); definitive diagnosis by microscopy alone is difficult because spore sizes overlap with head smut; no source found for a molecular method.

diseases.intro: No Korean source confirmed. No official Korean disease name or Korean occurrence record was found, and 'isak-kkambugi-byeong' is a provisional name. Everything below is an overseas description.

features.description: The disease is not apparent until tassels and ears emerge.
features.short_quote: "not evident until the tassels and ears appear"
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Sori form on tassels and ears, and rarely on leaves. Sori are compact masses of blackish-brown to black chlamydospores, covered by a thin grayish-white membrane that soon ruptures. The powdery spores are quickly dispersed by wind and rain.
features.short_quote: "covered with a thin grayish white membrane which soon ruptures"
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Tangled thread-like strands, remnants of the inflorescence vascular tissue, extend among the sori. This is characteristic of the disease. Vascular strands surrounded by blackish-brown spore masses distinguish it from common smut.
features.short_quote: "vascular strands... distinguishes head smut from common smut"
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Infected tassels are wholly or partly covered by sori and usually produce no pollen. Individual florets are completely replaced by chlamydospores without gall formation. Gall formation is characteristic of common smut.
features.short_quote: "replaced entirely by teliospores without the formation of a gall"
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Leaf-like and husk-like structures proliferate from the ear (phyllody). Streaks filled with chlamydospores form on leaves.
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Chlamydospores are diploid, reddish-brown to black, globose to subglobose, with many prominent spines, 9–14 µm in diameter. In soil they directly produce dikaryotic infection hyphae or form basidia. Sporidia are unicellular, haploid, hyaline and subglobose, 7–15 µm.
features.short_quote: "reddish brown to black, globose to subglobose, abundantly and conspicuously spiny"
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Sporidia of compatible mating types fuse to form infection hyphae that infect seedlings. Hyphae spread systemically into the seedling meristem, then into undifferentiated ear and tassel tissue, converting part or all of it into sori. Chlamydospores in soil survive 3 years or more.
features.growth_stage: Infection at seedling stage, expression at flowering
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: Low soil moisture (15–25% w/w) is optimal for seedling infection (part of the original sentence is garbled). Temperature is more important than soil moisture for infection. It is more common in clay loam than in sandy or silt loam and worse with nitrogen deficiency.
features.source_name: Illinois RPD 203

features.description: The 'galls' on tassels and ears are at first covered by a thin tissue layer that then ruptures, exposing black spore masses and thread-like vascular remnants. Leafy proliferation occurs on tassels and ears.
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia: Head Smut of Corn

features.description: Ears may degenerate and be replaced by proliferating leaf tissue, and plants may be severely stunted. There is a photo caption showing ear tissue replaced by leafy proliferation and spore masses.
features.short_quote: "Ears may be aborted and replaced with a proliferation of leafy tissue."
features.source_name: CPN Head Smut

features.description: Ears and tassels are replaced by sori filled with chlamydospores. Tassels show wire-like vascular protrusions, and ears show finger-like proliferation. Infected ears are teardrop-shaped, lack silks, and are filled with chlamydospores inside the husks.
features.short_quote: "wire-like extensions of the vascular bundles in the tassel"
features.source_name: Univ. Nebraska-Lincoln CropWatch: Head Smut

features.description: The fungus survives as thick-walled black chlamydospores. Unlike common smut, the chlamydospores are not inside fleshy galls. Infection is systemic from the seedling stage but becomes evident only on flowering plants. Infected ears and tassels are usually sterile.
features.growth_stage: Infection at seedling stage, expression at flowering
features.source_name: UNL CropWatch

features.category: Symptoms - tassel / Symptoms - ear/grain / Symptoms - leaf
features.description: Sporulation sites are tassels, ears and rarely leaves. The galls are rough and, when ruptured, expose dry spore masses mixed with strands of vascular tissue. Usually the whole ear is replaced by spores, but some ears bear a few kernels. Tassels are wholly or partly infected, sometimes limited to spikelets or proliferating into bizarre leaf-like structures.
features.short_quote: "dry spore masses with strands of vascular tissue"
features.source_name: PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Corn – Head Smut

features.description: In some hybrids stunting is the main symptom. Ears degenerate, or only a vestige bearing leafy buds remains instead of a normal ear. If only the ear is infected, the tassel is sterile.
features.short_quote: "Dwarfing may be a dominant symptom in some varieties."
features.source_name: PNW Handbook

features.description: Spores survive in soil for at least 5–7 years. Infection is said to occur at the seedling stage, but greenhouse studies found infection even several weeks after sowing. After infection it spreads systemically. Infection occurs even at a soil temperature of 15 °C (59 °F) and more readily at 20–30 °C (68–86 °F). It is not transmitted inside seed but can be carried on the seed surface.
features.growth_stage: Seedling stage to several weeks after sowing
features.source_name: PNW Handbook

features.category: Symptoms - tassel / Symptoms - leaf / Symptoms - whole plant (overseas original paper)
features.description: Introduction: tassels and ears are partly or completely replaced by 'large white galls containing blackish-brown spores', with stunting, loss of apical dominance and increased tillering. Results: tassel symptom types differ by line: (A) the whole tassel is charred, showing black threads and abundant spores; (B) spore-free leafy clustered structures form; (C) spores only at the base. Chlorotic spots appear on leaves at VE–V8.
features.growth_stage: VE-V8 (leaf spots), V12-VT (period when tassel symptoms are determined)
features.source_name: Wang et al. 2024, *Plants* 13(2):238 (China)

features.description: Incidence in northern China is 7–35%, up to 80% in some areas (cited in the introduction). The resistant line Mo17 averaged 1.5% over 5 years, while susceptible Huangzao4 averaged 88.7%.
features.source_name: Wang et al. 2024

features.description: Gives the forma specialis name "*Sporisorium reilianum* f.sp. *zeae* (Kühn) Langdon and Fullerton" for the head smut pathogen of maize and sorghum (PubMed abstract).
features.source_name: Sabbagh et al. 2008, *Commun. Agric. Appl. Biol. Sci.* 73(2):101-8 (PMID 19226747)

source_conflicts: 'Gall' terminology: Illinois says florets are replaced by spores 'without gall formation' and UNL says chlamydospores are 'not in fleshy galls', but CPN, PNW and Wang 2024 also call this disease's sori 'galls'. The common distinguishing points are 'no fleshy swollen gall' and 'vascular threads present'.
Membrane: Illinois 'thin grayish-white membrane', CPN 'thin tissue layer', Wang 2024 'white galls', which overlaps in color with the white membrane of common smut.
Chlamydospore figures (9–14 µm, reddish-brown to black, many spines) appear only in Illinois and overlap with the range for common smut (8–12 µm).
Survival in soil: Illinois 3 years or more, PNW at least 5–7 years.
Infection timing: Illinois and UNL 'seedling stage', while PNW adds infection several weeks after sowing in the greenhouse.
Scientific names diverge: CPN and UNL *Sphacelotheca reiliana*, PNW *Sporisorium reilianum*, Illinois *Sporisorium holci-sorghi*, Sabbagh 2008 *S. reilianum* f. sp. *zeae*.
diseases.photo_visible: Tassels and ears replaced by blackish-brown spore masses without galls, mixed with thread-like vascular remnants; leafy proliferation of ears (phyllody); teardrop-shaped silkless ears; stunting.
diseases.lab_required: Reddish-brown to black spiny chlamydospores 9–14 µm (microscopy; overlaps with common smut), molecular separation method (no source found).

diseases.scientific_name: Fusarium verticillioides and other FFSC species
diseases.intro: There is a Korean official source (Nongsaro 'isak-sseogeum-byeong' (ear rot), with the pathogen given as *Gibberella fujikuroi*) and two Korean original papers (Choi 2018 on FFSC in Korean grain, Han 2015). The rest of the symptom descriptions are from US extension sources.

features.description: Early on, ear husks and kernels are partly pink or reddish-brown. As it progresses, pinkish mold grows in cottony clumps on kernels and husks.
features.source_name: Nongsaro pests by crop: Ear rot (D00001173)

features.description: Mold grows especially around insect holes and wounds. With late infection, white streaks may form on the kernel pericarp.
features.source_name: Nongsaro D00001173

features.description: Common in warm, slightly dry weather. It occurs mainly on ears wounded or bored by birds or insects rather than healthy ears. Susceptibility of Korean cultivars is not well known. It also occurs during storage.
features.source_name: Nongsaro D00001173

features.description: Diseased kernels are scattered on the ear or clustered. They are especially common on kernels damaged by European corn borer, corn earworm and birds. Kernels turn purple, tan or brown. When mold is visible it is white to pink or purple.
features.short_quote: "Diseased kernels are scattered or in patches on the ear"
features.source_name: CPN-2001 *An Overview of Ear Rots* (2024 revision)

features.description: White streaks may form on kernels, called the 'starburst' symptom. It results from the pathogen growing beneath the kernel pericarp (seed coat).

The fungus survives on crop residue and spreads readily by windborne spores. It infects seedlings and developing kernels and can grow in stalks and ears for a time without symptoms or signs. Airborne conidia infect via silks or insect wounds, and soilborne conidia via roots. White to pink or purple cottony mold can form anywhere on the ear.

Occurs in many environments, but the most severe outbreaks are in warm areas and in fields with heavy insect or hail damage. Fumonisin levels rise when wet, warm weather continues just before harvest. Fumonisin levels can be high even when disease does not look severe. Table 1 gives the conditions as 'moderate to warm temperatures at silking, wet period before harvest'.
features.short_quote: "fumonisin concentration... can be high even when the disease does not appear to be severe"

features.description: The only reliable way to confirm ear rot or mycotoxins is often laboratory testing. If unsure, submit samples for laboratory diagnosis. Scouting starts at late dent (R5).
features.short_quote: "A lab test is often the only reliable way"

features.description: The most common ear disease, caused by several *Fusarium* species. White to pink or salmon-colored cottony mold forms on one or several kernels, scattered or in clusters. Rot often starts at insect-damaged kernels, and infected kernels are tan or brown or have white streaks.
features.short_quote: "white to pink or salmon-colored, cottony mold"
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia: Fusarium Ear Rot of Corn

features.description: The causal fungi overwinter in maize residue and dead grass weeds. Spores reach silks by wind and rain splash and also infect through kernel wounds made by insects and others. Insects also act as vectors. *F. verticillioides* can grow throughout the plant and may reach the ear via the stalk. High temperature and dryness at and after silking are favorable.
features.source_name: CPN Fusarium Ear Rot

features.description: White to peach or purple cottony mold forms on one or several kernels scattered over the whole ear. Infected kernels are tan or brown or show starburst white streaks. Symptoms vary with genotype, weather and severity. In severe cases the ear is almost consumed, and the lightened husks are bound to the kernels by mycelium.
features.source_name: Univ. Tennessee UT Crops: Fusarium Ear Rot (H.M. Kelly)

features.description: Occurs under a wide range of weather conditions, but is most severe with temperatures above 25 °C (77 °F) and a wet period before harvest. Infection occurs at silking, but spread continues after R6 until grain moisture falls below 18%. The optimum temperature for fumonisin production is 75 °F (about 24 °C).
features.source_name: UT Crops

features.description: The most common causal fungi are *F. verticillioides*, *F. proliferatum* and *F. subglutinans*. Of these, *F. verticillioides* and *F. proliferatum* are associated with fumonisin production.
features.source_name: UT Crops

features.description: The maize pathogen *F. verticillioides* produces abundant, mostly single-celled microconidia in characteristic long chains by enteroblastic phialidic conidiogenesis.
features.short_quote: "mostly single-celled microconidia in distinctive long chains"
features.source_name: Glenn, Richardson & Bacon 2004, *Mycologia* 96(5):968-80 (PMID 21148918)

features.description: Microconidia of *F. verticillioides* occur in two forms, chains and false heads. In mutants lacking the hydrophobin genes *HYD1* and *HYD2*, chains were rare and almost only false heads formed. That is, chain formation is a trait that can change at the gene level.
features.source_name: Fuchs, Czymmek & Sweigard 2004, *Fungal Genet. Biol.* 41(9):852-64

features.category: Pathogen morphology (comparison table; soil isolates, not maize)
features.description: *F. verticillioides*: microconidia are ovoid, aseptate, in long chains of more than 20. Macroconidia are slender, 3–5-septate and rare. Conidiogenous cells are monophialides, and there are no chlamydospores. Pigment is white to dark or pale purple. *F. proliferatum*: microconidia vary in shape and form chains of 11–15. Monophialides and polyphialides occur together, and false heads also form. No chlamydospores; pigment white to pale violet.
features.source_name: Karim et al. 2016, *Trop. Life Sci. Res.* 27(1):1-20 (isolates from Malaysian peat soil)

features.description: *F. temperatum* isolated from ear-rot ears (pink or white mold) in Jilin, China: colonies on PDA are white and cottony at first, becoming pinkish-white. Microconidia are hyaline, 0–2-septate, obovoid to ovoid and do not form chains. No chlamydospores. Macroconidia are falcate, 3–5-septate (mostly 4) with a foot-shaped basal cell. Identification was confirmed by TEF-1α sequence (100% match).
features.source_name: Zhang et al. 2014, *Plant Dis.* 98(9):1273 (First Report, China)

features.description: In 2011–2015, 878 FFSC isolates were obtained from Korean grains (barley, maize, rice, soybean) and identified by TEF-1α and RPB2 sequences. In maize, *F. verticillioides* 33.9%, *F. fujikuroi* 25.3% and *F. proliferatum* 21.1% dominated. All isolates of *F. fujikuroi*, *F. proliferatum*, *F. verticillioides* and *F. thapsinum* were *FUM1*-positive. Of 19 *F. fujikuroi* isolates, 16 produced more than 1000 µg/g fumonisin (FB1+FB2) on rice medium.
features.source_name: Choi et al. 2018, *Int. J. Food Microbiol.* 267:62-69 (RDA National Institute of Agricultural Sciences)

features.description: The List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004) records ear rot caused by *Gibberella fujikuroi* and stalk rot caused by *F. moniliforme*. The *G. fujikuroi* species complex, formerly called *F. moniliforme*, has been shown to be a species complex of several species. Korean stalk-rot isolates were identified as *F. subglutinans* and *F. temperatum* by morphology and EF1α sequencing (stalk rot, not ear rot).
features.source_name: Han et al. 2015, *Res. Plant Dis.* 21(4):280-289

source_conflicts: Mold color: Nongsaro 'pink, reddish-brown, pinkish cottony' (no mention of white or purple), CPN-2001 'white to pink or purple', CPN 'white to pink or salmon', UT 'white to peach or purple'. Nongsaro's 'reddish-brown' overlaps with Gibberella's 'pink to red'.
Starburst: Nongsaro mentions only 'white streaks with late infection', while CPN-2001 and UT explain that it is caused by fungal growth beneath the pericarp.

Weather conditions (largest difference): Nongsaro 'warm and slightly dry', CPN encyclopedia 'high temperature and dryness after silking', CPN-2001 Table 1 'moderate to warm at silking, wet before harvest', UT 'above 25 °C and wet before harvest'. They are compatible if dryness during infection and wetness before harvest (increasing fumonisin) are treated as different stages.
Distribution: CPN-2001 'scattered or clustered', UT 'scattered', and Nongsaro mentions only 'around insect holes and wounds'.

Scientific names: Nongsaro *G. fujikuroi*, US sources *F. verticillioides* and others. Choi 2018 reports that *F. fujikuroi* makes up 25.3% of FFSC in Korean maize and produces high fumonisin levels, so which species the Nongsaro name refers to cannot be determined from symptoms.

Microconidial chains: Glenn 2004 and Karim 2016 'long chains', Zhang 2014 *F. temperatum* 'no chains', Fuchs 2004 'changes even with a single gene'; the only morphology table comes from soil isolates, not maize (Karim). Nongsaro gives no pathogen morphology.
diseases.photo_visible: White to pink or purple cottony mold scattered around insect- or bird-damaged kernels, starburst white streaks on kernels, tan or brown discolored kernels.
diseases.lab_required: Species identification within FFSC (TEF-1α, RPB2), fumonisin concentration (toxin analysis; can be high even with mild symptoms), *FUM1* production capacity (molecular), microconidial chains (microscopy, culture).

diseases.intro: There is a Korean official source (Nongsaro maize 'red mold disease' document) and a Korean FGSC original paper (Lee 2012). Sources differ on whether the Korean name 'bulgeun-gompangi-byeong' (red mold disease) refers to ear rot or stalk rot.

features.description: Occurs on ears at harvest and during storage. At harvest, infection mainly starts at the ear tip, discoloring and rotting inward. During storage, kernels discolor and rot at any part of the ear.
features.source_name: Nongsaro maize pest document 'Red mold disease (Gibberella)' (attached doc, kidofcomdtyNo=29198)

features.category: Symptoms - ear/grain / signs (husks adhering, red color)
features.description: Severely diseased ears rot entirely together with the husks. Abundant pink to red mycelium and spore masses form between husks and ear. During storage, white mycelium covers the seed and later pink to red conidial masses form. Severe ears turn red overall and rot. Eating it causes poisoning in pigs and other livestock.
features.source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

features.description: Produces ascospores, conidia and chlamydospores. In nature the ascigerous stage is rare and mainly conidia are produced. No microconidia, only macroconidia. Macroconidia are sickle-blade-shaped, 3–7-septate, 25–62 × 2.5–5.0 µm. Chlamydospores are hyaline to pale brown, globose, 10–12 µm in diameter.
features.source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

features.description: Optimum growth temperature is 24–26 °C. No description of colony pigment (Unconfirmed).
features.source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

features.description: Overwinters as asci, conidia and mycelium on diseased ears and husks, then causes primary infection. Lesions produce conidia again for secondary infection. Disease starts at silk formation and continues through harvest into storage. Frequent rain at silk formation favors infection and severe disease.
features.source_name: Nongsaro Gibberella (red mold) disease document

features.description: Pinkish mold often starts at the ear tip. On severe ears the mold binds the husks and silks tightly to the ear, called 'mummified ears'. Unless the hybrid is highly susceptible or conditions extreme, only part of the ear is attacked.
features.short_quote: "pinkish mold that often begins at the ear tip"
features.source_name: CPN-2001 *An Overview of Ear Rots* (2024 revision)

features.description: Relatively easy to recognize in the field on intact ears, but much harder after shelling. DON or zearalenone levels can be high even when disease does not look severe.
features.short_quote: "much more difficult to identify after the grain has been shelled"

features.description: Overwinters on maize and small-grain residue and can also infect soybean roots. Spores produced on residue cause infection at silking. Rain splash and spores discharged from special structures infect via silks or the ear base. More common when cool and wet at early silking. Worse when autumn rains delay harvest. Most severe in continuous-maize fields and areas with wheat head blight. Table 1 summarizes the conditions as 'cool, wet' and the symptom as 'pink to white mycelial growth'.
features.short_quote: "Red or pink mold forms, typically beginning at the ear tip."
features.location_in_source: 'Gibberella Ear Rot' paragraphs 2-3, Figure 7 caption, Table 1

features.description: Most easily recognized by the red or pink color of the mold. Almost always starts at the ear tip. With heavy mold, silks and husks stick to the ear, and in severe cases pink mold is visible on the outside of the husks at the ear tip. A photo of disease on a hail-damaged ear is included.
features.short_quote: "It almost always begins at the tip of the ear."
features.source_name: CPN Encyclopedia: Gibberella Ear Rot of Corn

features.description: The fungus overwinters on maize residue, and spores spread by rain splash and wind to infect via silks. Silks are most susceptible 2–6 days after emergence. Common when cool and wet during grain fill.
features.short_quote: "Silks are most susceptible two to six days after emergence."
features.source_name: CPN Gibberella Ear Rot

features.description: The fungus infects mainly through the silk channel, producing pinkish-white mold at the ear tip. Cool, wet weather (rain or high relative humidity) during and after silking (R1) is optimal. The same pathogen also causes stalk rot and wheat head blight.
features.short_quote: "pinkish-white mold to develop at the tip of the ear"
features.source_name: Ohio State Univ. Fact Sheet AC-52 (Willyerd, Paul, Mills, Thomison)

features.description: Kernels with similar visible mold can differ in internal colonization and toxin production. Kernels that look healthy can also be contaminated. Black light cannot detect vomitoxin, which does not fluoresce. ELISA is toxin-specific, so zearalenone and aflatoxin need separate tests. A rule of thumb is not to feed grain with more than 5% moldy kernels.
features.source_name: OSU AC-52

features.description: Pink to red mold starts at the ear tip and progresses toward the base. Pinkish mold is generally diagnostic of this disease. Severe ears are mostly rotted with husks and silks tightly bound, and pink to red mold may grow between husks and ear. Except in highly susceptible hybrids, only part of the ear is attacked.
features.short_quote: "begins at the tip of the ear and develops toward the base"
features.growth_stage: Just before harvest (best time for scouting)
features.source_name: Purdue Extension BP-77-W *Gibberella Ear Rot* (Woloshuk & Wise)
features.location_in_source: p.1 'Scouting and Identifying', Figures 1-2; p.2 first paragraph

features.description: Common when cool and wet during the first 21 days after silking. At grain moisture above 22% and about 80 °F, fungal growth and toxin production continue inside the ear. Cold periods below 50 °F can increase zearalenone production. Spread and toxin accumulation stop when grain moisture falls below 18%. The presence and amount of DON can be determined only by chemical analysis.
features.short_quote: "Only a chemical analysis can verify the presence and amount of" DON
features.source_name: Purdue BP-77-W
features.location_in_source: p.1 introduction; p.2 'Mycotoxin Testing'; p.3 'Minimizing Economic Losses'

features.description: The sexual stage of *G. zeae* forms purple to black perithecia, a distinguishing feature of the genus *Gibberella*. Ascospores are usually 3-septate, slightly shorter and thicker than conidia, without a foot cell. No microconidia; only one type, macroconidia. Macroconidia are banana-shaped, 3-septate when mature, with the foot cell typical of *Fusarium*. Conidial masses are pink. (Description centered on wheat head blight)
features.short_quote: "produces only one kind of conidia - macroconidia"
features.source_name: Hallen & Volk, Tom Volk's Fungus of the Month (Univ. Wisconsin–La Crosse; aug2005 page)

features.category: Pathogen (Korean FGSC composition; molecular, toxin type)
features.description: 568 *F. graminearum* isolates from maize at 8 Korean locations were analyzed by AFLP, identifying lineages 2, 3, 6 and 7. Proportions were lineage 7 75%, 6 12%, 3 12%, 2 1%. Sexual fertility (female fertility) was lineage 7 100%, 6 70%, 3 26%, 2 14%. All lineage 3 and 7 isolates produced DON, while most lineage 2 and 6 isolates produced NIV.
features.source_name: Lee et al. 2012, *Appl. Environ. Microbiol.* 78(7):2161-7 (PMC3302601)

features.description: FGSC isolates from ear rot in Chongqing, China were divided by TEF-1α sequence into 16 *F. meridionale* and 3 *F. asiaticum* isolates. Identification was based on 'morphological and molecular' results, with TEF-1α sequences analyzed when species-specific PCR was inconclusive.
features.source_name: Zhou et al. 2018, *Toxins* 10(2):90 (China)

features.description: The List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004) records it as "red mold disease caused by *G. zeae* (Gibberella stalk rot)" (secondary citation). The English name is given as stalk rot.
features.source_name: Han et al. 2015

source_conflicts: Certainty of starting at the ear tip: CPN encyclopedia 'almost always', CPN-2001 'often, typically', Purdue 'from tip toward base'; Nongsaro says 'mainly' the tip at harvest but adds the caveat 'at any part' during storage.

Mold color: Nongsaro pink to red (white mycelium then pink to red in storage), CPN red or pink, OSU pinkish-white, Purdue pink to red. The 'white' element means its color overlaps with Fusarium ear rot.
Infection route: CPN, OSU and Purdue 'silks'; CPN-2001 Figure 7 'silks or ear base'.

Weather: all US sources say 'cool and wet', but the period wording differs (early silking, 21 days after silking, grain fill, after R1); Nongsaro gives only 'frequent rain at silk formation' and a fungal growth optimum of 24–26 °C.
Macroconidial septa: Nongsaro 3–7 (25–62 × 2.5–5.0 µm), Volk page '3-septate when mature'. The Volk page centers on wheat head blight.
Korean name: the Nongsaro maize document uses 'red mold disease' for the ear disease, but the English name in the List of Plant Diseases in Korea (2004, cited by Han 2015) is 'Gibberella stalk rot'.
diseases.photo_visible: Pink to red mold spreading from the ear tip toward the base, mummified ears with husks and silks stuck on, pink to red mycelium between husks and ear.
diseases.lab_required: DON and zearalenone concentrations (chemical analysis only; black light does not work), FGSC species and lineage and DON/NIV toxin type (AFLP, TEF-1α), identification of shelled or stored samples (culture, molecular).

diseases.intro: No Korean source confirmed. EPPO lists Korea as 'Present, few occurrences', but the basis is a single 2010 detection on *Dracaena sanderiana* in a greenhouse in Gyeonggi, not a maize record. Everything below is an overseas description.

features.description: There are no Korean symptom data or occurrence records on maize. EPPO lists Korea as "Present, few occurrences", but the basis is a single 2010 detection on *Dracaena sanderiana* in a greenhouse in Gyeonggi.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, ERWIST distribution KR

features.description: Susceptible sweet corn hybrids wilt quickly (wilt phase). Dent hybrids are generally resistant to the wilt phase. Plants die at the seedling stage, or if infected late may grow to some extent.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: Sweet corn infected early is most severely affected. Young plants wilt, are stunted, and show water-soaked lesions with wavy margins.
features.source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)
features.location_in_source: End of p.2 Injury paragraph (sweet corn)

features.description: Sweet corn: pale green to yellow longitudinal streaks with irregular or wavy margins that can run the full length of the leaf. Streaks turn brown as they dry.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: Dent corn: short or long irregular pale green to yellow streaks **starting from flea beetle feeding scars**. Diseased areas, sometimes whole leaves, turn straw-colored.
features.short_quote: "start at corn flea beetle feeding marks"
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: Lesions start at feeding scars (small scratches). They are pale green to yellow streaks at first and turn brown as tissue dies. Margins are usually wavy but follow the veins overall. The photo description mentions water-soaked wavy margins.
features.source_name: Crop Protection Network, Stewart's Disease of Corn (posted 2026-09-24) (CPN-Stewart)
features.location_in_source: Body symptom paragraph and photo descriptions

features.description: Severely infected plants may develop **cavities in the stalk pith near the soil line**. Weakened plants are more prone to stalk rot.
features.short_quote: "Cavities may form in the stalk pith"
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: When the stalk is infected the whole plant wilts.
features.source_name: Crop Protection Network, Stewart's Disease of Corn (posted 2026-09-24) (CPN-Stewart)

features.description: Tassels emerge early, bleach, and wilt and die before the rest of the plant. Small irregular water-soaked spots form inside and outside the husks and darken as they dry. Small droplets of exudate may form on inner husks.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: Drought worsens the disease. As a result ears are often small or absent.
features.short_quote: "small ears or no ears at all"
features.source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

features.description: Bacteria penetrate deep into the seed but do not reach the embryo. Dent corn kernels are rarely infected unless disease is severe and the hybrid susceptible.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: When an infected stalk or leaf is cut across, **masses of yellow bacterial slime** emerge.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: Viewing a lesion section at about ×100 or more shows bacteria streaming (ooze) from the vascular bundles.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: When an infected stalk is cut, **pale yellow bacterial droplets** may seep out.
features.source_name: Crop Protection Network, Stewart's Disease of Corn (posted 2026-09-24) (CPN-Stewart)

features.description: Adults spread the bacteria while feeding. Bacteria accumulate in and block the vascular bundles, interfering with water and nutrient movement. Infection can occur at any time during growth, and there are two phases: seedling infection (wilt phase) and infection after tasseling (leaf blight phase). Most commercial field corn is resistant to the wilt phase but somewhat susceptible to the leaf blight phase.
features.source_name: Univ. of Illinois IPM, Corn Flea Beetle Insect Fact Sheet (UIUC-CFB)

features.description: Seedlings are mainly infected by vector feeding, and secondary spread occurs during summer.
features.source_name: EPPO Global Database, *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii* datasheet (EPPO-ERWIST)

features.description: Field corn shows few symptoms until late summer, after which many leaf lesions form. In years with many flea beetles, some hybrids wilt and die before tasseling. Under suitable conditions, almost 100% of susceptible field corn hybrids show symptoms by late autumn.
